data.title: The consensus among Fed hawks is heating up, with two figures advocating for a move of over 25 basis points in December.
data.description:
Author: Xiao Yanyan, Jinshi Data

Support for further tightening of monetary policy within the Federal Reserve is increasing. The minutes of the October 27-28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, released Wednesday, show that **almost all participating officials believed that interest rates may still need to be raised in the coming months** to ensure that inflation falls back to the 2% target level in a timely manner.

The minutes stated, "In the coming months, almost all participants believed that, based on their baseline forecasts of inflation and the labor market, it may be necessary to further raise the target range for the federal funds rate to ensure that inflation returns to the 2% target level in a timely manner."

Among them, **two policymakers proposed a more aggressive rate hike plan. They believed that if subsequent inflation data performed poorly, the December rate hike might need to be "more than 25 basis points."

This reflects broad support within the Federal Reserve for further interest rate hikes, but the specific magnitude and pace of these increases remain points of contention among policymakers. The Federal Reserve's October meeting decided to maintain interest rates unchanged by a 10-2 vote. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted against a 25-basis-point hike. Previously, the Fed had raised rates by 25 basis points in September, its first rate hike in three years. The meeting minutes also revealed that several officials who supported keeping rates unchanged in October believed the decision "almost changed." However, other officials in the majority believe that market expectations for further rate hikes in December and 2027 are "broadly consistent" with their assessment of the appropriate monetary policy. They believe these expectations also reduce the risks associated with the Fed's decision not to raise rates in October. The disagreement extends beyond whether rates should be raised; it also concerns how the Fed should communicate its future policy direction to the market. The meeting minutes show that some officials who supported an October rate hike appeared dissatisfied with the Fed's previous policy communication methods. They stated that they might have supported maintaining the current interest rate, but only if market participants clearly understood that further tightening of monetary policy was likely in the future. The disagreement among officials focuses on the magnitude of rate hikes and policy signals. Comments made earlier on Wednesday by Fed Governor Christopher Waller also indicate that some officials support accelerating policy tightening. In an interview with CNBC, Waller stated that he supports a 50-basis-point rate hike by the Federal Reserve in December. He later added that if this 50-basis-point increase were to be implemented in two phases, in December and January, policymakers would need to send a "credible signal" to the market that another rate hike would occur in January. However, other officials do not share the same view on the pace of rate hikes. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly stated on Wednesday that the Fed should take a cautious and prudent approach when raising rates. Fed Governor Michael Barr also stated that further rate increases might be appropriate. In contrast, New York Fed President John Williams on Tuesday dismissed the idea that the Fed needs to consider a large rate hike. Interest rate futures currently reflect investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates by 25 basis points each in December and January, followed by another rate hike in April. This market pricing indicates that investors have already priced in continued rate hikes over the next few months, but policymakers still have differing opinions on the magnitude and timing of each hike. Inflationary pressures and a weak housing market create a policy tug-of-war. Inflation data further strengthens the case for rate hikes. October consumer price data shows that price increases have spread to more everyday consumer goods and services. A portion of wholesale prices is included in the Fed's preferred inflation measure, and these prices saw their fastest year-over-year increase since 2022 in October. However, continued interest rate hikes could have a greater impact on some sectors of the economy that are highly dependent on borrowing, including the housing market. Data released this week highlights the weakness in the US housing market. Last month, existing home sales fell to their lowest level in 16 years. Sluggish housing activity is also a reason for some officials to advocate for a cautious approach to interest rate hikes. When the Federal Reserve makes its interest rate decision in October, the US midterm elections are also in their final days. However, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh previously told reporters that he did not hear any discussion about the elections during the interest rate decision meeting. AI investment becomes a new risk variable. Federal Reserve officials' concerns about inflation have expanded from factors such as energy and tariffs to more areas of the economy. The meeting minutes show that officials generally agreed that "inflationary pressures in the economy are widespread," thus necessitating further action. AI investment was also listed as one of the core topics of discussion. Policymakers noted that AI-related demand "will pose a significant inflation risk." The Fed staff briefing officials also warned that complex financing arrangements between AI companies could amplify industry risks, including off-balance-sheet lease commitments and revolving financing structures. These arrangements could further amplify losses should related investments fall short of expectations. The minutes stated: "Most participants noted that AI-related debt is growing rapidly, and a significant portion of this growth comes from complex and opaque financing structures. A few participants noted that AI-related risk exposure is increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few companies." This means that the Fed's focus on the AI ​​boom is no longer limited to inflationary pressures from infrastructure investment, but also includes issues such as corporate debt growth, financing transparency, and the concentration of financial risks. However, officials still expect inflation to fall sharply in 2027 and beyond as the effects of the current shock gradually subside.

data.title: ChatGPT partners with Visa and others: Do agents still need stablecoins?
data.description:
Re-examining the relationship between traditional payment networks, stablecoins, and the Agentic Economy.

The narrative of the integration of AI Agents and Web3 is sparking a debate.

On November 13th, OpenAI announced the launch of ChatGPT Wallet and partnered with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to enable agents to complete purchases and payments on behalf of users.

On November 13th, OpenAI announced the launch of ChatGPT Wallet and partnered with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to enable agents to complete purchases and payments on behalf of users.

Previously, AI agents were considered the most promising emerging use case for stablecoins. However, OpenAI chose to integrate with traditional bank card networks as its first step in implementation, leading many to question, "If even ChatGPT is integrated with Visa and similar services, do agents really still need stablecoins?" This questioning is not without merit, but it actually confuses two different concepts: "Agentic Commerce under human authorization" and "Agentic Economy of machine autonomous collaboration." For current agent applications primarily focused on shopping, booking, and daily consumption, funds still originate from human users' bank accounts. Transactions heavily rely on the mature merchant networks, identity verification, and consumer protection mechanisms of the bank card system. Traditional payment networks clearly possess a more mature commercial infrastructure. However, the boundaries of the Agentic Economy extend far beyond this. When AI begins to autonomously purchase data, call APIs, lease computing power, and even engage in continuous value exchange with other agents, payment needs may no longer be limited to traditional consumption scenarios. Therefore, the key question is that the Agentic Economy is not equivalent to Agentic Commerce, especially when AI transforms from a human consumption assistant into a participant in economic activities. What kind of payment and financial infrastructure is truly needed? I. Why Traditional Finance as the First Stop for Agent Payments? To understand why OpenAI chose Visa and Mastercard, it's essential to clarify two often confused concepts: Agentic Commerce and Agentic Economy. The former primarily refers to AI replacing humans in consumer behaviors such as product discovery, price comparison, ordering, and payment; the latter is a broader concept, meaning that AI agents can not only execute tasks assigned by humans but may also operate independently of individual human instructions, engaging in continuous transactions with other agents, businesses, and service providers. From the current implementation progress, Agentic Commerce is clearly leading the way, while traditional card organizations still hold an unshakeable advantage in this field. Taking ChatGPT Wallet's design as an example, it is actually quite restrained and pragmatic. Users pre-link eligible bank cards. When the agent finds the target product and is ready to pay, the user views the product, total price, and selected bank card, and confirms the transaction through security verification such as Face ID or fingerprint. Subsequently, the payment network will provide a set of payment tokens to replace real bank card information to complete the transaction. Merchants and agents do not need to directly access real bank card information, and users can continue to enjoy their original bank card rewards and eligible transaction dispute protections. The biggest advantage of this design is that it does not require users to change their existing payment habits, nor does it require merchants to build a new payment system. After all, for AI products targeting mass consumers, directly reusing Visa and Mastercard's global merchant acceptance network, acquiring system, and anti-fraud risk control is far more realistic than educating ordinary users to "buy stablecoins first, then create an on-chain wallet, and finally manage gas fees." More importantly, traditional payment systems not only handle fund transfers but also provide a complete commercial dispute resolution mechanism—when goods have quality issues, consumers can file a chargeback appeal, and merchants can continue using existing refund and customer service processes. This is a capability that on-chain payments currently lack in the global retail sector. However, there is a detail that is easily overlooked: ChatGPT Wallet has not yet achieved completely unattended autonomous payments; users still need to manually check and verify each transaction beforehand. According to OpenAI's initial design, users still need to confirm the goods, total price, and bank card before each purchase and complete authorization through biometrics. Future plans include further opening up pre-authorization capabilities, allowing users to pre-set spending limits, purchase categories, and validity periods, enabling agents to complete transactions autonomously within a defined scope. This precisely illustrates that consumer-grade agents are still in an early stage of "human-led, AI-assisted" development. AI merely assists humans in purchasing goods; therefore, the existing bank card system can already solve most problems. However, if an agent needs to call APIs thousands of times daily, purchase real-time data, lease GPU computing power, and pay service fees to other agents, then it faces no longer a simple shopping problem. II. Penetrating the Agentic Economy: Where are the Opportunities for Stablecoins and New Protocols? When AI Agents evolve from "assistants that help people buy things" to "economic entities that autonomously conduct business," the transaction structure will undergo a qualitative change. Imagine a company deploying an AI research agent. To complete a deep analysis task, it might need to perform a series of actions in parallel within minutes: purchasing real-time market data from a data service provider, leasing GPU computing power from a cloud computing platform, calling third-party AI models to complete the analysis, purchasing professional data processing services from other agents, and finally delivering the results. Throughout the process, the Agent needs to establish payment relationships with multiple different service providers. Compared to traditional consumer payments, this type of transaction exhibits several distinct characteristics: **Fineer Transaction Granularity:** In the past, enterprises typically purchased APIs, data, and computing resources using subscription, pre-paid, or package models. However, when the Agent can dynamically invoke different services based on task requirements, pay-per-use and pay-per-call billing become more natural; **Higher Transaction Frequency:** An Agent can run continuously for hours, or even remain online for extended periods, transacting with multiple service providers. It cannot wait for manual payment information to be entered by humans every time a service is invoked; The transaction relationships are becoming more open: different agents may operate on different companies, in different countries, and on different technology platforms, without traditional account relationships, and may not share the same bank or payment service provider; Cobo's Head of Sales and Solutions, Lucas, previously shared a sampling study of the Base and Solana networks at the 4th Cross-Border Digital Finance Compliance Conference: in a sample covering 35 days and over 6 million transactions, over 90% of AI-related payments were only a few cents, or even less than 1 cent (further reading "When AI Agents Begin Autonomous Payments: Cobo Lucas Talks about Stablecoin Payments and Security Infrastructure"). This data reflects that some early machine payments have already shown a clear characteristic of small amounts. Similar practices are emerging: weather query APIs charging less than 1 cent per use have appeared on the Solana network, along with token security screening services charging a few cents per use; on the internet content side, infrastructure giants like Cloudflare are also promoting pay-per-use mechanisms based on the x402 protocol, allowing AI crawlers to settle accounts with content providers in real time for each webpage crawled. Traditional bank cards are not incapable of handling small transactions, but when payments shift from occasional consumption to high-frequency, automated API calls, the costs associated with authorization, payment processing, and settlement for each transaction can become a bottleneck to business efficiency. In other words, only blockchain networks and stablecoins can make this high-concurrency, extremely small-amount machine-to-machine (M2M) settlement economically viable. In addition, stablecoins also offer a more programmable settlement method suitable for the Agentic Economy. In this model, payments can be directly embedded into the Agent's automated task flow via smart contracts and APIs. Agents can hold stablecoins in their wallets and, upon authorization, make payments to designated addresses. They can also interact with smart contracts to complete more complex fund management operations, without relying on traditional bank card accounts and merchant acquiring processes for every machine-to-machine transaction. For example, in computing power or API scenarios where fees are charged per second, stablecoins support 24/7 circulation. Enterprises can also combine them with payment flow protocols (such as Superfluid) to achieve continuous settlement on a per-transaction, timed, or per-second basis, without having to wait until the end of the month for unified reconciliation. Of course, this doesn't mean that stablecoins are cheaper or more efficient than bank cards in all scenarios. On-chain transactions still involve issues such as network fees, liquidity, fiat currency deposits and withdrawals, compliance screening, and merchant acceptance. What's truly important is that stablecoins provide an internet-native, programmable way to transfer value, enabling payments to integrate more naturally into automated machine collaboration. Overall, the industry has recently developed several clear protocol routes surrounding machine-based autonomous payments, and even traditional card organizations are actively embracing this dual-track approach. These include Coinbase's x402, Stripe and Tempo's Machine Payments Protocol (MPP), and Google's AP2. While their focuses differ, they all attempt to solve a common problem: how to enable agents to initiate and complete payments autonomously, much like calling an API. Several noteworthy developments have occurred this year: On March 18, Visa released dedicated payment specifications and an SDK, enabling agents to use tokenized bank card credentials in machine payment processes, signifying that traditional card payments are also beginning to adapt to API calls and inter-machine transactions; On June 3, Mastercard announced the addition of the option to use regulated stablecoins for on-chain settlement in its existing global payment network, involving assets such as USDC, PYUSD, USDG, USDP, and RLUSD, as well as multiple networks including Ethereum, Solana, and Base; On October 10th, Visa launched its AI-powered business infrastructure, including Agent Score and Agentic Directory, at the Payments Forum, while also expanding its stablecoin settlement pilot program. On October 15th, Visa Direct and Mastercard both advanced the commercialization of stablecoins—Visa moved its USDC pre-deposit capability from pilot to commercial deployment for cross-border payments; Mastercard, along with its acquired stablecoin infrastructure company BVNK, launched the Global Money Platform, integrating fiat and stablecoin accounts through a single API, enabling real-time exchange, stablecoin-linked bank card transactions, and local bank withdrawals. From October 19th to 20th, Mastercard further penetrated stablecoin risk control and automated payments, launching Stablecoin Security, which combines payment data with blockchain analytics to provide financial institutions with pre-transaction risk identification, and showcasing Agent Pay for... Machines, based on x402, allows agents to purchase digital services and uses digitally signed payment credentials to achieve authorization, execution, and settlement. These actions demonstrate that traditional payment networks and blockchain are not simply in competition. Visa, at the 2026 Payments Forum, summarized this trend with the statement: "AI is changing the front end of commercial transactions, while stablecoins are reshaping the back end of fund flows." The future of the Agentic Economy may not be about one payment method replacing another, but rather the gradual integration of different payment tools, protocols, and settlement networks.

III. Stablecoins are not the only option, but programmable trust infrastructure is a must

Returning to the initial debate: Do agents still need stablecoins?

The answer is actually very clear: stablecoins are not the "only" way for agents to make payments, but when transactions become open, high-frequency, and cross-entity collaborative, they provide a programmable settlement option suitable for the agentic economy.

A more fundamental question than payment methods is: when AI gains the ability to use funds, who ensures it doesn't exceed its authorized scope? This may be more important than choosing a payment method. Ordinary consumers using bank cards only need to manage their own accounts and spending habits, but future businesses may deploy multiple agents simultaneously, each responsible for procurement, transactions, fund allocation, supplier payments, and risk management. If each agent has unrestricted wallet access, the enterprise is effectively distributing control of funds among multiple automated programs. More complexly, even if the server isn't compromised and the private key itself isn't leaked, an agent influenced by misinformation or malicious instructions could still initiate payments beyond the user's true intent within a legitimate transaction process. Therefore, the core of Agentic Wallet isn't simply assigning a wallet or bank card to AI, but rather separating the AI's autonomous execution capabilities from the enterprise's control over funds. Taking Cobo Agentic Wallet as an example, to allow multiple agents to autonomously use funds within controllable boundaries, a layered mechanism from key management to transaction authorization needs to be established. First, there's MPC (Multi-Party Computation), which separates signing authority to avoid single points of control. Cobo Agentic Wallet further designs two signing participation mechanisms: Agent + Cobo handles automated transactions within the authorized scope, while Human + Cobo handles high-value approval and governance operations. No single participant can independently complete a signature. Second, there's Pact, which defines the boundaries of Agent action through task contracts. Cobo's Pact authorization framework transforms each task into an executable authorization protocol for the underlying infrastructure, primarily comprising four elements: operational intent (what goal the agent is authorized to achieve), execution plan (the steps the agent intends to take to complete the task), policy constraints (allowed budget, transaction objects, chains, tokens, contracts, and approval rules), and completion conditions (automatic termination of authorization upon task completion, budget exhaustion, or expiration of the valid time). The agent first generates a Pact draft based on user instructions, which is then reviewed and approved by the user. After the task is initiated, each transaction is verified according to the rules in the Pact; only operations fully complying with the authorized scope will trigger the Cobo collaborative signature node to release them. This fundamentally changes the traditional approach of AI security relying on natural language instructions. In the past, we were accustomed to telling AI what it could and couldn't do through prompts, but large models' understanding of natural language always had uncertainties. By implementing permission constraints at the wallet and signature infrastructure level, security rules are no longer just "suggestions that AI should follow," but become hard prerequisites for transactions to execute. Finally, in addition to key management and permission constraints, agents also need reliable execution paths. Cobo encapsulates common on-chain tasks into predefined execution templates through Recipes, covering contract interactions, parameter restrictions, and operational processes—for example, an agent can use the corresponding Recipe to complete Uniswap transactions, Aave deposits, Superfluid continuous payments, and call paid APIs that support x402. If MPC addresses who can sign, and Pact addresses what the Agent can do, then Recipe addresses how the Agent should reliably complete its tasks. These three aspects correspond to key security, access control, and execution reliability, respectively, collectively forming the basic security framework for Agents using funds. Of course, from Agent wallets to enterprise payments, a complete financial operations system is also required. Lucas has also proposed a practical approach for enterprise integration: enterprises can choose stablecoin payment infrastructure from two dimensions. One dimension is the asset management method, namely third-party custody or self-custody; the other dimension is the system access method, namely standardized payment page, or embedding into existing business systems via API or SDK. These two options can be flexibly combined according to the company's business needs, technical capabilities, and compliance requirements. This modular approach means that traditional payment institutions do not have to choose between completely relying on third-party service providers and building their own on-chain system from scratch. Instead, they can retain their existing payment systems and key business processes while simultaneously accessing the necessary on-chain asset management and payment capabilities. From this perspective, the financial infrastructure needed by the Agentic Economy is no longer just a wallet or payment channel, but a system comprised of key management, access control, payment protocols, fund settlement, compliance screening, and financial operations. In conclusion, the emergence of ChatGPT Wallet is actually a signal that the Agentic Economy is beginning to enter the real-world business system. In the consumer market, bank cards and established card organizations still possess irreplaceable advantages in terms of experience and trust. However, for API calls, data purchases, computing power leasing, and machine-to-machine transactions, stablecoins and other programmable payment methods offer new possibilities. Future agents will not be limited to a single payment tool; they may complete transactions via bank cards, purchase on-chain services using stablecoins, and complete corporate settlements based on bank accounts. Therefore, stablecoins may not necessarily replace Visa, and Visa and similar entities may not monopolize everything. However, as long as agents begin to participate in economic activities, the programmability provided by blockchain will become an optimal settlement option outside of Visa's existing system. However, regardless of the channel through which funds flow, when the users of assets shift from "carbon-based humans" to "silicon-based intelligent agents" on a large scale, verifiable identity authorization, programmable risk control boundaries, and a traceable foundation of trust will always be prerequisites for the Agentic Economy to achieve large-scale development. About Cobo Founded in 2017 and headquartered in Singapore, Cobo builds trustworthy wallets and payment infrastructure for humans and AI agents, with licensed entities in Hong Kong, Canada, and the United States. Cobo has passed SOC 2 Type II (Big Four audits) and ISO 27001 certifications, has had zero security incidents since 2017, and has protected billions of dollars in customer assets.

data.title: Crypto Payment Compliance Map: Why is it still not working even though all the licenses have been obtained?
data.description:
When crypto payment projects reach a certain stage, licenses are usually not the first problem to surface. A company may have already obtained CASP authorization, completed FinCEN MSB registration, and connected with overseas licensed payment institutions, but operations will still be stuck in specific areas such as customer funds, wallet control, fiat currency accounts, and merchant settlement.

Once the business is truly operational, several problems will quickly emerge: institutions capable of handling digital assets may not be able to handle Euro payments; banks are willing to open operating accounts but do not accept long-term pooling of third-party customer funds; and the responsibilities of customer development, contract signing, wallet control, and transaction execution may be handled by different companies within the same group.

Thus, each company in the group has its own regulatory status, yet the entire transaction still cannot be completed smoothly. The number of licenses cannot solve this problem; the key is whether customers, assets, fiat currency, and responsibilities are aligned on the same executable business chain.

A license only answers whether an entity can engage in a specific regulated business.

Who receives the funds from the customer, who controls the stablecoin, who pays in Euros, why the bank accepts the funds, and who handles refunds or freezes—all these details need to be traced back to specific entities, contracts, accounts, and system permissions. Previous articles have discussed stablecoins in the US, Canada, Australia, the EU (MiCA CASP), Dubai (VARA), Hong Kong, and licensed partnerships. Returning to the actual operation of crypto payments, the question is quite simple: if every step has compliance arrangements, why can't transactions be completed? The key is to determine which entities, accounts, and systems the transaction actually passes through, not just the license list. Projects need to break down customer wallets, asset custody, stablecoin exchange, on-chain transfers, fiat currency payments, and merchant settlements, clearly specifying which entity performs each function, based on which authorization, and who bears responsibility for any problems. The project needs a table mapping business functions to regulatory identities: which entity completes each function (customer wallet, asset custody, stablecoin exchange, on-chain transfer, fiat currency payment, and merchant settlement), based on which authorization, and who bears responsibility for any problems. [Image: Six compliance checkpoints from transaction initiation to settlement completion (Source: Mankiw Law Firm)] 01 The license list doesn't reflect real business operations. The most common mistake a project makes is putting all the regulatory qualifications the group has obtained on the same promotional page and assuming these licenses cover all business operations. For example, a group might have an MSB registration in the US, a CASP authorization in Europe, and partnerships with licensed payment institutions in other regions. These regulatory identities are certainly valuable, but they are not simply additive. The US FinCEN MSB registration is not a uniform operating license covering all money transmission businesses in the US; specific activities still need to be determined in accordance with state laws. The EU CASP can enter other member states through MiCA's Passporting mechanism after completing the required cross-border notification, but the cross-border services it can provide are still limited to the original authorized scope of crypto asset services. It does not automatically acquire all the business rights of a payment institution or electronic money institution simply by completing Passporting. For stablecoin payment projects, the issue may be even more complex. On March 2, 2026, the transition period between MiCA and PSD2 previously set by EBA will end. Some electronic currency token (EMT) transfer and custody wallet services may also need to resolve payment service authorization issues. This means that projects cannot simply ask how many licenses the group has; they must confirm item by item: customer wallets, asset custody, stablecoin exchange, on-chain transfers, fiat currency payments, and merchant settlements, under which entity and which authorization. What projects need is a table mapping business functions to regulatory identities, not a list of group licenses. 02 Customer Relationships, Asset Control, and Funding Paths Don't Match Suppose a corporate customer is preparing to pay a European merchant. The customer registers on the project's website, uploads company information, completes KYC/KYB, and then transfers stablecoins to the platform's designated wallet. The platform completes the exchange, and then transfers the Euros to the merchant's bank account through a payment partner. What the user sees may only be a single payment, but regulatory and banking due diligence requires reconstructing at least three distinct paths. The first path is the customer relationship path. Which company within the group did the customer sign the service agreement with? Did the customer purchase a digital asset exchange service, a funds transfer service, or a complete cross-border payment service? In the event of refunds or complaints, which entity should be responsible? The second path is the crypto asset control path. To which address do the customer's stablecoins go? Who controls the private key? When are the assets transferred to the CASP or liquidity provider? Who has the authority to decide on transaction execution, and who bears the responsibility for protecting customer assets? The third path is the fiat currency funding path. To whose account do the converted USD or Euros go? Is that account authorized to receive such funds? Who ultimately executes payments to merchants, and can banks identify the actual payers and payees? If a client signs a contract with a European CASP, but their assets and fiat currency are controlled by other entities without the corresponding business authority for an extended period, the project needs to re-examine the actual service provider and their legal responsibilities. If the contract specifies technical services, but the technology company actually receives client funds and decides on transactions, the contract title alone cannot be used to conclude that it is completely free from financial regulation.

Figure: Three paths for a cross-border stablecoin payment (Source: Mankiw Law Firm)

03 ​​Having a license doesn't necessarily mean banks are willing to accept transactions

This is where the previous issues tend to surface.

Companies may have obtained regulatory approval and found partner institutions that can provide fiat currency services, but they still cannot establish stable payment and receipt accounts.

The reason is not necessarily that banks do not accept the crypto asset industry, but may be that the purpose of the account proposed by the project cannot be approved by the bank.

For example, a bank allowing a business to open an account for salaries, rent, and normal operating expenses does not mean that the account can be directly used to receive payments from multiple third-party clients. Similarly, a licensed institution's ability to handle specific types of financial transactions does not mean that its banking partners have approved all client regions, transaction amounts, funding sources, and merchant categories. The European Banking Authority (EBA) emphasizes that financial institutions should assess the actual risk of their clients and should not excessively de-risk entire client categories without sufficient justification. However, banks still need to comply with anti-money laundering requirements and decide whether to establish or continue business relationships when they cannot effectively manage the relevant risks. Therefore, even if a project is licensed, it needs to explain to the bank: what the account is specifically used for, how client funds are generated, whether the transactions correspond to genuine business activities, the on-chain asset processes, and how the company identifies and handles abnormal transactions. If this explanation doesn't hold water, continuing to add licenses may not solve the account opening problem. A license can prove that a business has a legal basis for operation, but banks still need to determine whether they can bear the risks of that business entering the account system. Therefore, truly mature licensing planning should not wait until the license is approved before seeking banks. Account types, payment and receipt paths, clearing methods, and the business access scope of bank partners should be considered simultaneously when designing licenses and group entities. 04 Many licensed partners, but no one is responsible for the complete transaction. The crypto payment industry has formed a large number of mature infrastructure cooperation models. Wallets can be connected to third parties, identity verification can call KYC service providers, exchanges can be handled by liquidity institutions, and fiat currency payments can be handled by PIs, EMIs, or banks. This division of labor itself is not problematic. For companies that don't intend to self-license in all markets, utilizing licensed institutions may even be a more efficient business choice. However, the more partners there are, the easier it is for responsibility to be diffused. For example, a customer payment might be suspended because an on-chain address triggers a risk warning. The wallet service provider believes it's only responsible for the technology, the CASP believes KYC is handled by the front-end platform, the payment institution believes the source of assets is not within its scope of verification, and the project team believes the entire process has been handed over to a licensed partner. If, only when an anomaly occurs in the transaction, do the parties begin discussing who has the right to freeze the transaction, who is responsible for explaining the situation, and who contacts the customer, it indicates that this cooperative relationship has not yet formed a truly enforceable responsibility arrangement. Article 73 of the MiCA sets forth clear requirements for CASP outsourcing: Companies may outsource operational functions, but they cannot transfer their regulatory responsibilities as a result, nor can outsourcing alter the relationship between the CASP and its clients or the terms of their authorization. Licensed partnerships must address interface access and revenue sharing, and clearly define the boundaries of responsibility. The partnership agreement must also specify client access, transaction instructions, asset control, compliance monitoring, anomaly handling, data sharing, complaints and refunds, regulatory inspections, and how to migrate clients after termination of the partnership. For regulated services already provided by the company itself, the partner's license cannot simply replace necessary authorization. Whether a service can be outsourced and whether regulatory responsibility can be delegated are two different issues.

05 Business Operations are Successful, but Sustainable Risk Control Fails

Some projects can complete test transactions and provide transfer and exchange services to a small number of customers, but they may still encounter significant obstacles after scaling up.

The reason is that completing a transaction and operating a financial business long-term have different requirements.

Early-stage projects may only serve a small number of corporate clients, and the source of transactions and the purpose of funds are relatively clear. However, as the platform begins to cover more countries, increase the number of merchants, support self-custodied wallets, or connect to multiple liquidity providers, the risk management requirements will also change accordingly.

In July 2026, the FATF released its seventh update on the implementation of regulations governing virtual assets and service providers, paying particular attention to the abuse of stablecoins, transactions related to self-custodied wallets, offshore VASPs, DeFi arrangements, and the difficulties in the actual implementation of the Travel Rule.

This means that compliance for crypto payment projects cannot stop at completing a KYC upon account opening or purchasing an on-chain analytics tool. Projects need to continuously identify customers and counterparties, monitor abnormal transactions, comply with applicable Travel Rule information requirements, and handle risks related to sanctions, fraud, and suspicious funds. A more practical question is: what happens if a transaction cannot be executed or a bank refuses to settle after customer funds have entered the platform? If a partner institution suddenly stops providing services, can the platform promptly identify affected customer assets and arrange refunds or other legal disposals? A truly mature risk control system should cover before a transaction begins, during execution, and after a transaction fails. 06 Before Launch, Conduct a Complete Stress Test with a Single Transaction Instead of checking all licenses and regulatory documents together, it's better to choose a typical business scenario for the project's launch and simulate it from start to finish. For example, an Asian company uses a stablecoin that complies with applicable regulatory requirements to pay a European supplier, who ultimately receives Euros. The project needs to answer the following questions one by one, following the actual business process. [Image: Six stress tests before a crypto payment project launches (Source: Mankiw Law Firm)] If any questions cannot be answered, the project cannot claim to have fully met the requirements for launch, nor can it use other licensing procedures to cover up this shortcoming. Some problems cannot be solved simply by adding a license. A bank's refusal to accept certain types of customer funds may require adjustments to account and transaction structures; unclear responsibilities within a group may necessitate redefining the contracting and asset control entities; and a partner's lack of access to transaction data requires modifications to system permissions and agreement arrangements. For businesses, this method of inspection is closer to actual operations than simply comparing the number of licenses. 07 Multi-License Collaboration, Three Essential Diagrams A company preparing to conduct global encrypted payment business long-term does not necessarily need to establish completely independent business systems in every market. However, it must ensure that different regulatory bodies can work together according to clear rules. A more reasonable planning approach can be divided into three phases.

Figure: Three-stage implementation path of multi-license synergy (Source: Mankiw Law Firm)

Stage 1: Design business, then choose regulatory path.

The project needs to clearly define which countries the main clients are located in, where the funds come from, where the final settlement is located, and whether the product involves issuance, custody, exchange, fund transfer, or traditional payment services.

On this basis, it can be determined which qualifications the group needs to hold and which businesses can be completed through licensed cooperation.

Phase Two: Simultaneous Design of Licenses, Accounts, and Funding Paths. Companies should determine the client contracting entity, asset control method, bank account purpose, payment partners, and internal/external service agreements during the main structure stage, rather than adding a separate company for each license obtained. For projects planning to expand into multiple markets in the future, local customer access, cross-border service restrictions, and business license scope should be considered in advance. Phase Three: Validating the Entire Structure in Real Transactions. Before large-scale official launch, representative clients and transaction types should be selected, and the consistency of fund flow, information flow, and responsibility flow should be verified according to the approved testing schedule. The ability to handle abnormal transactions, partnership interruptions, refunds, and customer complaints should also be checked. The focus is not on completing a single successful payment, but on confirming that the entire business can be continuously executed in real-world operations. When to obtain a license, when to cooperate, and when to adjust the business structure. Conclusion: Licenses must ultimately become executable payment paths. From US MSB, Canadian MSB, and Australian DCE, to El Salvador's DASP, Cayman's VASP, and then to the EU's MiCA, Dubai's VARA, Hong Kong's stablecoins, and multi-license collaboration, we discussed the regulatory paths of different countries and regions in the "Global Crypto Payment Compliance Map." These systems each have their own characteristics and correspond to different market and business needs. However, if you look at the whole series together, you will find that one question runs through it all: A crypto payment project needs to solve not only what a certain country allows it to do, but also how to connect different countries, different financial institutions, and different business functions. A single MSB registration cannot replace a state-level license, a single CASP cannot automatically cover all fiat currency payment services, a VARA license cannot directly solve all payment token issues, and having multiple licensed partners does not guarantee that banks will accept related funds. Projects should not pursue a large number of licenses, but rather the integrity of their operational structure. Who is the service provider for the customer, who legally holds and transfers assets, who executes the exchange and payment, why can the bank accept the funds, and who bears responsibility in case of anomalies? Only when these questions are clearly answered can a license truly transform into business capability. The ultimate goal of global crypto payment compliance is not for every company to obtain the most licenses, but for every transaction to be completed through a legal, clear, and sustainable path. This is also the core question that the entire "Global Crypto Payment Compliance Map" series aims to answer. This concludes the main series of "Global Crypto Payments Compliance Map." Moving forward, we will continue to monitor global stablecoin regulation, digital asset payment infrastructure, AI agent payments, cross-border settlements, and related regulatory changes, conducting in-depth research on emerging legal and commercial issues.

data.title: Approximately $3.8 million in losses: Kava Lend vulnerability analysis and stolen funds tracking
data.description:
On November 14th, Kava Lend, the native lending protocol on the Kava blockchain, was attacked. The attacker exploited the lending module's supply calculation and settlement mechanism to lend out a total of 55,205,050.601443 KAVA (worth approximately $3.8 million). Beosin's analysis of this attack is as follows: I. Vulnerability Analysis To understand this attack, it's necessary to distinguish three important concepts in Kava Lend: Cash: A type of asset actually held by the module account, determining how many real tokens can be transferred out at any given time. Total Supply: Cash + Borrows - Reserves, used as the denominator in the supply interest distribution. User Deposit Claim: The user's withdrawable balance recorded in the protocol, updated according to the supply interest index.

The source code with the vulnerability is as follows:

func CalculateSupplyInterestFactor(newInterest, cash, borrows, reserves sdk.Dec) sdk.Dec {
   totalSupply := cash.Add(borrows).Sub(reserves)
   if totalSupply.IsZero() {
       return sdk.OneDec()
   }
   return (newInterest.Quo(totalSupply)).Add(sdk.OneDec())
}

When When totalsupply is a very small positive number, even a small amount of interest can generate a huge growth factor. Therefore, an attacker only needs to achieve the chain of very small net supply → abnormal interest growth factor → global supply index surge → user deposit claims expansion to create huge claims out of thin air and lend out funds far exceeding their deposits.

II. Attack Process Analysis

(1) The attacker used the main wallet kava1uzx5924cqsutcw365ajs8kkc3rr4vtlyzms255 to submit 37 MsgRepay transactions in the same transaction, repaying all the loans in the BUSD market at that time. (2) Subsequently, the main wallet executes a transaction in which it deposits 3,801.60356061 BUSD, lends out 1,267.20118686 BUSD, and withdraws 1,267.20118686 BUSD, keeping the net supply used to allocate supply interest at 0.00000002 BUSD.

https://www.mintscan.io/kava/tx/D5D8F728D9E11569B3FA40744FF1580BA3EF18C504F0382FE590149E683E337F

(3) The BUSD supply interest rate index rose from approximately 2.76 to 671,186.99, an increase of approximately 243,000 times. The BUSD deposits originally held by the main wallet were thus updated to a book value of approximately 1.25449 billion BUSD. The attacker used the main wallet to deposit BUSD and withdraw excess BUSD funds to profit.

https://www.mintscan.io/kava/tx/C59113E2E5C9C0B45782814F3190679A25C8DBA6ACA36B3B0C6BC0433FE02509

（4）The attacker borrowed KAVA using BUSD through a second wallet kava1v2s266sll8ca5xrs06swmsc00nwwt7u77eufk4. Through multiple rounds of borrowing and liquidation, approximately 55.2 million KAVA were eventually extracted.

III. Tracing Stolen Funds

According to Beosin Trace's analysis, after the attackers transferred the KAVA they obtained back to their main wallet, they used LayerZero to cross-chain to BNB Chain and sell it. Most of the stolen funds were transferred to the BNB Chain address 0x37d732914f86cc6eb1e87419e3046a739f011042.

After the attackers converted the funds into BNB, they used the cross-chain protocols Li.Fi and Chainflip to exchange the BNB for ETH on the Ethereum network, totaling 384.72 ETH.

... The attackers then dispersed the funds to multiple addresses, using Across to transfer the majority of the ETH to Arbitrum, and then swapped the ETH for USDC, ultimately transferring it to Hyperliquid. The attackers' addresses have been flagged, and Beosin Trace will continue to monitor the movement of all stolen funds.
