data.title: Revenue soared to hundreds of billions: Huang Renxun was rebuffed by the board of directors?
data.description:
Nvidia, which has been surging ahead in the AI ​​wave, recently released a financial report that can only be described as "unbelievable."

But even more explosive than the financial report is the "power struggle" circulating within the company—it is said that Jensen Huang wanted to return to Nvidia as CEO, but was ruthlessly rejected by the board of directors?!

Soaring Performance: Revenue of $115.8 Billion, Simply Unbeatable

Let's take a look at this report card that has left Wall Street speechless.

According to the announcement on Nvidia's official website (parallel universe version), revenue in the third fiscal quarter (ending October 25, 2026) reached a staggering $115.8 billion! A 20% increase quarter-over-quarter and a staggering 103% increase year-over-year.

It's worth noting that LSEG analysts had previously projected $109.1 billion, making this a truly exceptional performance. The core data center business remains a "cash cow," generating $107.6 billion in revenue, a 110% year-over-year increase. Non-GAAP earnings per share were $2.68, and the gross margin remained a solid 74.9%. Nvidia even boldly predicted that fourth-quarter revenue would reach $130 billion, and note that this doesn't even include data center revenue from China. Following this news, Nvidia's stock rose approximately 2.7% in after-hours trading. Plot Twist: Huang's heartfelt appeal, the board's cold response. Logically, with such strong performance, the CEO should be treated like royalty. However, this report took the form of a prime-time business drama. According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, Jensen Huang suddenly broke his silence in a statement. He not only expressed being "deeply moved" by the outpouring of support, but also released a shocking signal: he is willing to return to the position of CEO of Nvidia! Wait a minute, has Huang been ousted? Even more dramatic is the response from Nvidia's board of directors. Faced with the founder's "job application," the board stated, "We have no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO." Furthermore, the report also mentioned an "interim CEO" named Colette Kress. This interim leader calmly stated in the earnings call that revenue for fiscal year 2028 is expected to grow by approximately 75% year-over-year, higher than the previous expectation of 70%.

data.title: Former New York Fed President Dudley: Painless inflation cuts are doomed to fail
data.description: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has been hawkish in his rhetoric regarding the 2% inflation target, but his actual policy actions have been far more conservative—a discrepancy that former New York Fed President Bill Dudley has sharply criticized. He argues that the Fed's strategy of anchoring inflation expectations through hawkish statements to achieve a "painless reduction in inflation" lacks historical basis and has inherent logical flaws, making it doomed to failure. In a Bloomberg column on Tuesday, Dudley pointed out that inflation has been above the Fed's target for nearly six consecutive years, but monetary policy has not actually been restrictive. The Fed only raised the federal funds rate target in September, reversing one of its three rate cuts planned for 2025, and the current interest rate level is still about 75 basis points lower than the 2024-2025 average. Meanwhile, while financial conditions have tightened slightly, they remain loose overall. Models by Federal Reserve staff indicate that financial conditions will still contribute 0.8 percentage points to GDP growth over the next year. This discrepancy between words and actions has a direct impact on the market. Dudley warned that if the Fed does not take substantial tightening action, inflation expectations risk drifting upwards instead of falling back to the 2% target as officials have hoped. He expects a December rate hike to be almost a certainty, but this step alone is insufficient to bridge the gap between policy signals and actual actions. Strong rhetoric, delayed action. Warsh, in his press conference following the October 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, made clear statements emphasizing that the Fed is "fully responsible" for the 2% inflation target and explicitly denied speculation that the Fed was tolerating higher inflation. However, Dudley points out that there is a significant gap between policy reality and the aforementioned statements. The September rate hike was merely a partial pullback from previous easing measures, and the federal funds rate remains at a relatively loose level. Low unemployment and generally loose financial conditions do not support the judgment that "monetary policy has become restrictive." Dudley believes that this "talking the talk but not walking the walk" approach has continued for several years, and the fact that inflation has consistently failed to return to the target is itself a denial of the effectiveness of this strategy. Two Fatal Flaws of "Immaculate Disinflation" Dudley summarizes Warsh's implicit strategy as "immaculate disinflation"—that is, maintaining credibility through strong statements, thereby anchoring inflation expectations and allowing inflation to naturally fall back to 2% without causing a substantial shock to the labor market. Walsh himself stated, "I don't think we need to harm the labor market to achieve our goals." Dudley raised two fundamental criticisms of this. First, this strategy has been tested over many years and has failed. Inflation, without substantial monetary tightening, has not converged to the anchored inflation expectations as expected. Second, in the absence of actual policy follow-up, the logic can also work in reverse: inflation expectations do not anchor downwards but rather drift upwards, converging towards the actual inflation level. Surveys from the University of Michigan and the Household Survey both show that one-year inflation expectations are as high as 4.7% and 3.9%, respectively; even longer-term indicators reach 3.5% and 3.0%, respectively, still at relatively high levels. Supply shocks cannot be an excuse for inaction. Dudley also addressed another mainstream argument in the current policy discussion—that monetary policy is not a suitable tool for dealing with supply-side shocks such as tariffs and energy prices, because such shocks may be short-lived or one-off price level adjustments. He acknowledged that this argument has some merit, but argued that it overlooks a crucial point: the Fed's responsibility is to ensure that demand does not persistently exceed available supply. If a decline in supply leads to a relative surplus in demand, prices will rise, and the Fed will need to suppress demand to re-achieve equilibrium. He cited the experience of 2022-2023, pointing out that an extremely tight labor market did indeed push up wages and inflation, and the tightness of the labor market still has a substantial impact on the inflation outlook; the Phillips curve has not failed. Furthermore, if inflation expectations become further unanchored in this process, the Fed will need to exert greater pressure to suppress demand, and the policy costs will be higher. A December rate hike may be a turning point, but far from enough. Dudley predicts that a December rate hike is almost a certainty, which will help narrow the gap between words and actions and is a step in the right direction. However, he also emphasizes that Warsh needs to be more candid with the market about the policy path required to bring inflation back to the 2% target. This is not forward guidance, but a basic explanation of how monetary policy should respond to changes in the outlook for economic growth, employment, and inflation. In Dudley's view, if the Fed continues to substitute hawkish rhetoric for concrete action, the vision of "painless inflation reduction" will not only be difficult to achieve, but may also further derail inflation expectations, ultimately forcing policymakers to pay a greater price.

data.title: Are crypto assets still safe in the era of quantum computing?
data.description:
Written by: imToken

If one day a quantum computer can derive a private key from a public key already exposed on the blockchain in an extremely short time, will the cryptographic asset security system built on cryptography today still hold true?

For a long time, discussions about quantum computing in the crypto industry have mostly remained at the theoretical deduction level, acknowledging that the elliptic curve cryptography widely used by mainstream blockchains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum could potentially be broken by quantum computers with sufficient computing power in the future, but this is still quite far off.

In fact, by 2026, this issue had officially entered the engineering implementation stage—the Ethereum Foundation not only established a dedicated post-quantum security research team, but also set the engineering goal of achieving post-quantum resistance across the execution, consensus, and data layers of L1 by the end of 2029 in its latest protocol planning.

... For an open network with hundreds of millions of accounts, a massive asset base, and a complex application ecosystem, changing the cryptographic system is far more than a simple software upgrade. Especially from the perspective of ordinary users, the real challenge often lies not in "how to generate a new quantum-resistant private key," but in how to securely and seamlessly control existing accounts and assets while changing the signature algorithm. I. What is the real threat of quantum computing? To understand the impact of quantum computing on crypto assets, we first need to dissect the blockchain security system. Currently, Ethereum primarily relies on four types of cryptographic components to operate, serving account, consensus, data availability, and application-layer proofs respectively. These components address different problems and have varying exposures to quantum computing risks: ECDSA: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm used for ordinary user accounts to prove ownership of the transaction initiator; BLS: Signature algorithm used in Ethereum's PoS consensus layer, efficiently aggregating votes from hundreds of thousands of validators into a single signature; ZK-proof systems: Zero-knowledge proof systems used in applications such as Rollups; KZG: Multinomial commitment schemes for verifying Blob and Rollup data availability (DA); Among these, asymmetric cryptography, such as ECDSA and BLS, which are based on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, are the most vulnerable. As is well known, it is computationally nearly impossible for traditional computers to deduce the private key from the public key. However, fault-tolerant quantum computers running Shor's algorithm can theoretically solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem in polynomial time, thus compromising the security of public-key cryptography like ECDSA and BLS, which are based on relevant mathematical assumptions. Once the private key is recovered, attackers can directly forge legitimate signatures to transfer assets without stealing the mnemonic phrase or compromising the wallet client. Similarly, validator keys, protocol multisignature management permissions, and cross-chain bridge control keys also face similar long-term challenges. In contrast, hash functions, represented by Keccak-256, are more resilient to quantum computing. While Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speedup, it doesn't transform the exponential security problem into a polynomial-time solvable one like Shor's algorithm does. This also highlights a crucial, often overlooked detail: not all Ethereum accounts are equally vulnerable to quantum threats. The address of a regular Ethereum account (EOA) is derived from the public key through a Keccak-256 hash. Therefore, if one of your cold wallets has never initiated any on-chain transactions or publicly disclosed signatures off-chain, then only the hashed address is recorded on-chain; the complete public key is never exposed and remains protected by the one-way nature of hashing. However, if that address initiates even a single transfer or contract authorization, an attacker can reconstruct the complete public key through the publicly disclosed transaction signature, directly exposing it to the risk of future elliptic curve cryptography breaches. Of course, currently, no quantum computer with cryptographic cracking capabilities exists globally, and ordinary users have no need to panic and transfer assets. The Ethereum Foundation's post-quantum team has also repeatedly emphasized that fault-tolerant quantum computers with real threats still need to overcome a significant engineering gap in hardware scale and quantum error correction (further reading: "What Does Quantum Computing Really Threaten? A Crypto User Guide to the Post-Quantum Era"). However, the problem is that cryptographic migration itself takes many years. If preparations are only started when the threat actually emerges, it may be too late. II. What preparations is Ethereum making? In 2026, the Ethereum Foundation established a dedicated Post-Quantum Security team to coordinate the research and engineering implementation of post-quantum cryptography at the protocol layer. Unlike simply searching for a new signature algorithm, Ethereum is attempting to simultaneously upgrade its cryptographic system from three directions: the execution layer, the consensus layer, and the data layer.

1. Execution Layer: Freeing Accounts from Permanent Binding to a Single Private Key

For ordinary users, the most direct change comes from the execution layer.

The account authorization logic of traditional Ethereum EOA is relatively fixed, that is, users generate signatures using the secp256k1 private key, and the network verifies the validity of the signature through ECDSA.

This design is simple enough and has been verified over a long period of time, but it makes the identity of the account highly bound to a specific signature system. If ECDSA is no longer secure in the future, users will need to change the signature algorithm, but if it is just a simple change of a new private key, it often means generating a new account address, and existing assets, contract interaction records, and application relationships may also need to be migrated.

This is clearly not an ideal solution. To break free from this constraint, Ethereum is accelerating the development of native account abstraction, most notably EIP-8141 (further reading: "Native Account Abstraction + Quantum Threat Resistance: Why Hasn't EIP-8141 Become Ethereum Hegotá's Flagship?"). It attempts to separate transaction verification, actual execution, and gas payments into different execution stages, allowing accounts to determine the validity of a transaction through programmable logic. This helps accounts gradually break free from their fixed dependence on ECDSA private keys, achieve native key rotation, and leave room for the future introduction of different signature verification algorithms. Simultaneously, Ethereum is also researching post-quantum signature verification pre-compilation, enabling smart contracts and account verification logic to more efficiently natively verify new signature types. But this is only the first step. Since post-quantum signatures are typically much larger than traditional ECDSA/BLS signatures, Ethereum also needs to address the resulting data and computational costs. For example, EIP-8288 proposes using recursive STARK aggregation to compress the verification results of a large number of post-quantum signatures into more compact proofs, thereby reducing on-chain data and verification burden. 2. Consensus Layer: Replacing Traditional BLS with Hash Signatures Besides the execution layer, the consensus layer is crucial to the underlying PoS operating mechanism of the Ethereum network. Currently, PoS consensus heavily relies on the aggregation characteristics of BLS signatures. If directly replaced with ordinary post-quantum signatures, the massive signature size will significantly increase the costs of P2P network propagation, storage, and verification between nodes. To address this, Ethereum's Lean Ethereum roadmap proposes two noteworthy technical directions.

  • leanXMSS: A post-quantum signature scheme based on hash functions, planned to replace the BLS signature currently used by validators, eliminating elliptic curve dependency at its source;

  • leanVM: A minimalist zero-knowledge virtual machine designed for efficient aggregation of post-quantum signatures, attempting to compress the hash signatures of a large number of validators into compact proofs through quantum-resistant zero-knowledge proofs such as recursive STARK, ensuring quantum-resistant security while maintaining the bottom line of consensus performance;

This also illustrates that there is no universal algorithm for post-quantum upgrades; validator consensus and ordinary user wallets each need to be matched with the most suitable cryptographic tools.

This also illustrates that there is no "one-size-fits-all" algorithm for post-quantum upgrades; validator consensus and ordinary user wallets each need to be matched with the most suitable cryptographic tools.

3. Data Layer: KZG and ZK Proofs Also Need to Consider Quantum Security Besides account signatures and validator signatures, the data layer also faces long-term challenges. Ethereum has used the KZG multinomial commitment mechanism extensively in recent years, especially in terms of Blob and Rollup data availability. However, the security of KZG relies on mathematical assumptions related to elliptic curve pairings, so the impact of future quantum computing needs to be considered. Furthermore, at the application layer, some ZK proofs used in systems like Rollups also have similar issues, especially some SNARKs that rely on elliptic curve pairings, whose security assumptions may also be affected by Shor's algorithm. In contrast, STARKs built based on hash functions do not rely on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm assumption, thus possessing better post-quantum security properties. This means that post-quantum migration is not just a problem for Ethereum L1; it will need to be gradually extended to L2, Rollups, and various on-chain applications in the future. Looking at the timeline, the Ethereum Foundation, in its protocol priorities announced in September 2026, explicitly stated its goal of achieving post-quantum resistance in Ethereum L1 at the execution, consensus, and data layers by December 2029. Subsequent upgrade nodes will also gradually introduce infrastructure such as post-quantum public key registration, signature verification, consensus proof, and data commitment. This will be a long-term project involving the entire ecosystem. III. How can users securely complete asset migration? If the first two parts discussed how Ethereum solves underlying cryptographic problems, then for ordinary users, the most important question is: what should our wallets do when the existing signature system needs to be upgraded? This is far more complex than regenerating a private key. The first issue to address is account identity. For traditional EOA, there is a direct mathematical link between the account address and the public key. If a user directly uses a new post-quantum key system, they typically need to generate a new account identity and then transfer their existing assets. This brings a series of problems. Besides ETH and ERC-20 tokens, users may also hold NFTs, deposits and positions in DeFi protocols, and assets on different L2 networks. Some applications also record permissions, points, historical interactions, and identity relationships based on user addresses. If each cryptographic upgrade requires changing the account address, users would have to re-manage these asset and application relationships, resulting in very high migration costs. Therefore, the importance of account abstraction becomes apparent. It can **separate account identity from the underlying signing key as much as possible**, allowing accounts to determine who has the right to control assets through programmable verification logic. Theoretically, this means that users will have the opportunity to change the underlying signing algorithm while retaining their original account address, without having to move all assets to another address. This is also one of the capabilities that EIP-8141 aims to provide. Secondly, there is the migration between old and new keys. An ideal migration process should involve the user proactively authorizing the new post-quantum key to take over the account while the existing cryptographic system remains secure. For example, a wallet can first generate a new post-quantum key in a secure environment, and then authorize the update of the account's verification rules using the existing account's valid signature. If the original ECDSA private key remains secure, this process can proceed as a normal account upgrade. However, if quantum computers are capable of cracking existing private keys, the situation is entirely different. At this point, both attackers and legitimate users may have the ability to forge the original account's signature, making it difficult for the system to determine the rightful owner based solely on the old key. This is why early migration is so important. Furthermore, there is an even more challenging type of account—wallets that have been inactive for a long time, whose private keys have been lost, or whose owners are unaware of the need for an upgrade. These accounts may still hold substantial assets but cannot proactively complete the migration. Regarding these types of assets, whether they should be allowed to remain at their original addresses or frozen through protocol governance in the future remains controversial. Finally, and most easily overlooked, secure migration itself must not become a new entry point for attacks. When the entire industry begins discussing the quantum threat, attackers could exploit user panic by creating so-called "quantum security upgrades," "private key verification," or "asset migration" pages to trick users into entering mnemonic phrases and signing malicious authorizations. Therefore, future wallets must not only provide migration tools but also enable users to clearly identify the source of the upgrade, verify transaction content, and confirm which assets the new authorization logic controls.

In conclusion

From today's perspective, quantum computing is far from being able to directly threaten the mainstream blockchain cryptographic system.

But this does not mean that the industry can ignore it.

Ethereum's post-quantum roadmap actually illustrates that the future security of blockchain should not be based on the assumption that a certain cryptographic algorithm will never be broken, but should be based on the ability of the entire system to continuously upgrade and securely migrate.

For ordinary users, the role of wallets will also change as a result.

In the past, the core function of a wallet was to help users generate, store, and use private keys. In the future, it will also need to help users understand account risks, manage keys across different cryptographic systems, and securely upgrade accounts when necessary. This is not merely a change in signature algorithms, but an evolution of the wallet from a private key management tool to a long-term asset security management infrastructure. At least for today, users don't need to rush to migrate their assets for quantum computing, but for wallet developers and the entire crypto industry, the time truly worthwhile to prepare has already begun.

data.title: After the simultaneous plunge in both cryptocurrencies and stocks: Hold your positions, buy the dip, or wait?
data.description:
Both crypto and stock markets have been weak for the past two weeks; US stocks have closed lower for several consecutive days, with Nvidia falling more than 10% last week; Bitcoin fell below $70,000 a few days ago, when it was hovering around $65,000. The market is mainly divided into two opinions: buy the dip or wait and see. The SmartX Closed Beta public test, which just opened yesterday, will be introduced at the end.

SmartX Space Sharing

· Topic: After the Double Sell-Off in Crypto and Stocks: Hold Positions, Buy the Dip, or Wait?

· Host: Amelia (@Miacrypta, SmartX)

· Guests: David (@David_MetaWorld, Founder/CEO of SmartX); Chain Research Society (@lianyanshe, Data-Driven Trader); Lao Bai (@Wuhuoqiu, formerly an investment researcher at ABCDE and OKX Ventures, now an Amber Group Advisor)

What's driving this drop?

David

· Bitcoin dropped from around 75,000 to over 60,000 very quickly, and it's not simply a matter of liquidating long positions; in less than a week, it fell from around 78,000 to around 62,000 / 61,900.

He believes the core issue isn't a fundamental problem with Bitcoin or cryptocurrencies, but rather that after the decline in AI stocks, traditional financial institutions need to replenish their stock positions and margin, leading to a coordinated sell-off of the most liquid assets. The underlying logic is inflation, and market expectations of rate hikes next month, or even the next two or three policy meetings, have created a pessimistic outlook on future liquidity. There's no single "whom to listen to": different trading preferences and position sizes require different viewpoints. This is why they focus on personalization. He mentioned that SmartX's next step will be to match the market and traders to users' preferences and styles. Recently, the funding environment has been bearish. Macroeconomic data fell short of expectations, and after the market turned around, it began pricing in a December rate hike, even anticipating further rate hikes in January and March of next year, creating a tight environment; highly volatile assets like Bitcoin were initially under pressure. The real weakening occurred after the CPI release. From the high of 87,000, there was a sharp drop of approximately 28%, a magnitude rarely seen in Bitcoin's history. If we apply the previous cycle, the maximum pullback after reaching the MA120 should have occurred at the MA120, around 75,000. Many experienced investors added to their positions here, but the decline didn't stop there, exceeding expectations. He views the latter half as Bitcoin's correction in response to macroeconomic conditions and the US stock market. Regarding the AI ​​industry chain, he mentioned that after the Democrats removed Nvidia as a leading stock, the valuations of some tech stocks are now lower than some consumer stocks, which he considers an extreme view. On-chain: Short positions remain concentrated; Nvidia's short positions haven't been closed out much. Regarding smart money, an increase in overall short positions was observed before the decline, with short positions exceeding long positions. Bottoming signals (still being verified): The first bottom in this round is at 57,000; the second bottom is expected at 62,000. He values ​​fee rates and a decrease in open interest (long positions capitulating, a healthier market); Coinbase premiums are returning to normal. The downside is: stablecoins are still flowing out, Bitcoin ETFs are still flowing out, pressure remains, but the market is slowly grinding to a bottom. · Crypto strengthened last night: The Nasdaq fell about 2% yesterday, while Bitcoin surged to $65,000 intraday before stabilizing at $64,000. It won't look lower unless it breaks $64,000; $62,000 should be a medium-term bottom. · I agree with David's explanation of liquidity: Bitcoin has the best liquidity, so institutions will sell it first when they need to replenish margin; assets with off-exchange trading, such as gold and Bitcoin, also fell over the weekend before the US stock market opened. · What native crypto users truly like is high volatility + high liquidity. In the past, they didn't pay much attention to revenue and fundamentals, focusing more on narrative. This round of liquidity has been largely exhausted, and there's too much supply on the supply side (too many altcoins), making it difficult to achieve both high volatility and sufficient depth for a single asset. Many altcoins have been steadily declining after being listed on mainstream exchanges.

· After Hyperliquid emerged, people discovered that volatility could be supported by a US stock-oriented approach, relying on fundamentals rather than just stories; he believes Hyperliquid performed well in terms of fundamentals, funding, and liquidity.

· The "crypto-ification" of US stocks and the US stock-ification of tokens have provided crypto users with targets that offer both volatility and better fundamentals. He cited Micron, Intel, and SanDisk as examples, which can see their value halved or doubled within one or two weeks, exhibiting volatility comparable to the crypto market.

· Judging bull and bear markets: He admits his accuracy is poor and hasn't achieved financial freedom as a result. About 90% of the dozens of indicators he summarized in the previous round will become ineffective in the next round. Even the experts he respects in metaphysics, candlestick charts, and fundamentals haven't foreseen 62,000 this round. The relatively stable one is Bitcoin's four-year cycle, which can only serve as a vague reference for tops and bottoms.

**Taking Sides: Washout or Continued Decline?** The moderator asked the three to clearly state their sides. David: Both are possible. The long cycle is still ongoing, but we are still in a bear market. * After April 11th last year, the market fell from its peak to July/August this year, then rebounded. He had some doubts about the rebound at the end of July: he had about 65,000 contracts, worth approximately $2 million, and almost all of it was liquidated when it rose to $72,000. He remembers it was the news announced by Trump (he said it might be the Genius Bill or something similar), and the market rallied by nearly 8%–9% in about 15 minutes. * It only took seven or eight months to fall from $120,000 to over $60,000, and then it was treated as a bear market turning into a bull market; he felt it was too fast. Looking back, the surge from over 60,000 to over 80,000 in July was just short-term news, not a sign of a bear market turning bullish. The 83,000-84,000 range cleared out a wave of long positions; this move is more like a healthy pullback, and the cycle timeline hasn't yet reached the point of a bear-to-bull market transition. If Bitcoin can consolidate around 60,000 for the next month or so before rising again, it would be more like a cycle rotation. He recently experienced a large drawdown and reviewed which wave he misjudged. Chain Research Society: 62,000 is a double bottom, still being verified; we are not expecting new lows at present. By the end of the year, the probability of the price consolidating without breaking 62,000 is increasing, but this has not yet been verified. If Bitcoin can hold between 64,000 and 62,000, he is not expecting new lows. • Time Window: This can be seen within the next month at the latest. If it doesn't break 62,000 within this month, the cycle that started from 57,000 is basically confirmed, and it's unlikely to make new lows afterward. • Macroeconomic expectations are too high. Pricing five interest rate hikes is a bit outrageous. The macro environment doesn't support such a large increase in interest rates; employment and consumption will collapse first. Some positive information can't be released now because the market is already overly pessimistic. • Personal Mistake: Not decisively cutting losses when the bull-bear trend line was broken; too confident that the bull market had started. He compared it to the major pullback in March 2020: many people leveraged when Bitcoin reached over 10,000 before and after the halving, which is similar to this time when it was over 80,000 and they saw it reach 100,000. Even without the hacking incident, there would have been a significant pullback; this time, leverage, macroeconomics, the Nvidia scandal, and Binance-related events all converged, causing a double bottom at 62,000, exceeding everyone's expectations. We'll tentatively consider 62,000 as the double bottom for this round, and continue to monitor data. We are optimistic about the market outlook: prices and US stock valuations/earnings have reached relatively suitable levels. (Note: The translation here is questionable: Google "has fallen below Buffett's cost"). The long-term negative factors for Nvidia haven't been fully resolved, and he doesn't believe Nvidia has bottomed out, but many high-quality assets have shown signs of bottoming out. The hardware index may not have bottomed out yet; there's an opportunity to reduce holdings next year. Investment banks expect capital expenditures to decrease by about 20%, and valuation contraction may present a good entry point. He also mentioned a long-term reference point: US stocks are likely to rise after the midterm elections; the historical pattern of buying indices and the long-term upward trend of the stock market has not been broken. Old Bai: Looking at a four-year cycle, around 60,000 is likely the bottom range; use probability to express position size, don't go all in at once. Similar to David: The only indicator that hasn't failed yet is the four-year cycle. If you have the patience to only trade Bitcoin—sell at the end of 2017, buy at the end of 2018, sell at the end of 2021, buy at the end of 2022, and sell at the end of 2025—even if you don't sell at the highest point (selling at 17,000-18,000 in 2017, and 100,000-110,000 in 2025 is also acceptable), buying back after a year will still result in a significant increase. In October 2025, it was around 120,000, and it's been a little over a year now. According to the pattern, it should have bottomed out, so around 60,000 is likely the bottom range. Two approaches: First, a vague sense of right is more important than precise judgment. Whether the top was sold at 69,000, 65,000, or 60,000 isn't that important, and the difference between buying at 57,000, 60,000, or 65,000 isn't that significant either. If you believe it's a bottoming range, you can enter at the opportune moment. Second, use probability rather than "all in when you're sure it's bottomed out": If you believe the probability of a bottom is 70%, your position size should reflect that probability. If you were to reallocate your portfolio, how would you allocate it? David (assuming $1 million) Cryptocurrencies, especially Bitcoin, would likely make up more than 50% of the portfolio. • The US stock market is in a somewhat awkward position: He almost completely cleared out his US stock holdings two or three months ago (keeping only some he felt were not closely related to AI). Now he only trades within two to three weeks, focusing on swings or trends, and no longer holds for years. He felt AI stocks would fall two or three months ago, but the decline exceeded his expectations (he originally thought it might reach around 180-190). Now, if he were to allocate another 10%-20% to US stocks, it would be more inclined towards biopharmaceuticals or consumer goods; he mentioned that Apple barely moved during this downturn. • He keeps about 30% in cash, waiting to see what happens next. • He is half optimistic and half pessimistic about US stocks; about 80% optimistic and 20% pessimistic about Bitcoin. There's no need to obsess over the perfect entry point; ultimately, there's no fundamental difference between 3 million and 3.5 million.

Chain Research Society

· Crypto is inherently a cyclical industry, and now there's an opportunity for reallocation; if it jumps directly from 80,000, many will miss out. If the cycle can be confirmed by the end of the year, it will be a very good time to re-enter; altcoins should be approached with caution, as they are unlikely to outperform Bitcoin, and one should also be careful not to make the wrong choice.

· The US stock market isn't as pessimistic as it seems: the driver is still corporate profits, and as long as valuations aren't a major issue, pension funds and other capital will gradually return through regular investment. This round of valuation contraction has been too rapid, and bursting the bubble early might not be a bad thing. AI's cash flow and the industry/products themselves are not problematic; we're now roughly in the middle of the cash flow phase. The market is worried about debt and the possibility of not being able to repay long-term loans. As hardware prices fall, computing power costs decrease, which is actually beneficial to the profits and financial statements of AI software companies.

As long as the company's fundamentals are sound and it's still profitable, the stock price will rise in the long run. There's no need to over-bet on presidential changes, government rotations, or macroeconomic factors. He believes it won't become like the dot-com bubble, where narratives outweigh cash flow, leading to a 90% drop, because cash flow has now been validated and has a bottom line. Most AI computing power stocks have already halved from their peaks. If cash flow is sound and debt can be managed, it's worth buying some, but pay close attention to financial reports and fundamentals. • In the next year or so, US stocks won't be a focus. Aside from Circle in pension funds, his personal holdings are Intel and Novo Nordisk. • Overall, US stocks are still relatively high in the long term. He won't touch hardware companies like Nvidia, Micron, SanDisk, and SK Hynix. Intel: I feel it's been unfairly punished; its fundamentals aren't that bad. The current price is in the $150-$60 range. I'm optimistic about Intel's future competition with TSMC, and from the US government's perspective, Intel and Micron are the cornerstones of American manufacturing, somewhat like Huawei in China. In the medium to long term, its price shouldn't remain at this level, so I'm holding onto my holdings; I'm not too worried about further drops. Novo Nordisk: Mainly because it's fallen too much. Eli Lilly has already surpassed a trillion dollars, and telperidine is very popular, but I don't think semagropeptide is more than ten times worse. The current dividend yield is already very high, having fallen significantly from its peak, and there's some stabilization at the bottom, so I bought some. SpaceX: I might consider it if it falls below $100. Right now, I think it's a good product but not cheap. Counterfeit: Some are still underwater. He's been wanting to buy Hyperliquid but hasn't found a good price. He might buy if it consolidates at the bottom and reaches around 50-60. Currently, he holds Zcash, NEAR, and ENA, corresponding to the narratives favored by the US and Europe in this round: ENA is DeFi and USD1, NEAR is Intent, and Zcash is privacy. He admits he bought NEAR and ENA too early. Regarding Circle: He still sees downside potential in the short term (the terms with Coinbase, revenue, and P/E ratio haven't yet reached the "good target + undervalued" level), but this is a 20-year retirement fund, so he's patient. He compares Circle/stablecoins to Bitcoin in 2015-2016 or Ethereum in 2017: it's already very popular within the crypto community, but most people outside haven't used it or understand it; it might take another 5-10 years for it to enter daily consumption and agent economy payments. He's looking at expansion ten years from now, and 30-60 is the range he would buy in.

· Bitcoin probability combination (example: $1 million, believing there is a 70% probability that $60,000 is the bottom, and a 30% probability that it may fall to $50,000 or even $40,000): Use 40%-50% to buy spot Bitcoin in three or four installments around $60,000 and hold it; sell a portion of it as 3-6 month put options with a strike price of $50,000 (he mentioned that this is Duan Yongping's way of buying Apple at the bottom), if it does not fall to $50,000, you can collect about 5%-10% of the premium, if it falls, it is equivalent to buying Bitcoin at $50,000; use about 5%-10% to buy forward leap calls (e.g., at the end of 2027 or mid-2028, with a strike price of about $80,000), betting that it may reach $100,000 or the previous high of $120,000 in one to two years; and keep 10%-15% in cash, unless there are extreme market conditions. (He verbally corrected the wording of "selling calls / selling puts" midway through; the following is his final summary.) Approximately half spot, 10%–15% cash, about 30%–35% selling puts, and 5%–10% forward calls, used to express the judgment that the market has bottomed out at 70%.
